A thermometer read every 10 minutes: 18.2, 18.4, 18.9, …
Your step count, one number per day
A heart monitor, 500 numbers per second
Three properties matter: it's the same quantity each time, the readings are in order, and the spacing is known (every minute, every day). A list of numbers with a clock is a time series; a spreadsheet of unrelated facts is not.

What the DB data is at first

A table of events. One row per train per stop: train number, station, planned time, actual time, cancelled yes/no. Thousands of rows, each about a different train. That's a table, not a series — nothing is lined up on a clock yet.

How it becomes time series

You pick one thing and track it over time:

RE 7, arrival at Bochum, minutes late, one number per day
day:    1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8 ...
late:   2   8   0  12   3   9  15   1 ...
That row is a time series. Others you'd build the same way:

Today's RE 7 along its route: lateness at stop 1, stop 2, stop 3 … (one number per stop)
Bochum station as a whole: average lateness of all trains, one number per minute
The lift on platform 4: working (1) or broken (0), checked every 15 minutes
Weather at Bochum, every 10 minutes
Why the model wants it this way

Patterns live in the sequence, not in the rows: "late every weekday evening", "started drifting in March", "spike then recovery". The model's encoder reads sequences of numbers, the way a cardiologist reads an ECG strip — and then writes the sentence. Give it the table and it sees facts; give it the series and it sees behaviour.

The answer it learns from

One more series, yes/no per day: did the connection hold? Computed from the same table (actual arrival of train A + walking time ≤ actual departure of train B). That's the label the model is trained to predict and explain.

What are the different types of data columns which we get from DB? All the different types

Read a page, searched the web
Grouped by source, with the role each column plays for you (series, annotation, or lookup).

1. Historical stop events (piebro / Bahn-Vorhersage) — your core

The piebro monthly files carry 17 columns per train stop: station_name, xml_station_name, eva (unique station id), train_name, train_number, line_number, final_destination_station, delay_in_min, time (actual arrival or departure), is_canceled, train_type (ICE, IC, RE…), train_line_ride_id (one id per run), train_line_station_num (position along the route), arrival_planned_time, arrival_change_time, departure_planned_time, departure_change_time, and a stop id. Sample rows show train_type also covers S-Bahn, regional buses and EV (replacement services), not just trains.

Series come from: delay_in_min, planned vs changed times, is_canceled — lined up per train per day, or per stop along a ride via train_line_station_num
Static annotations: train_type, line_number, final destination, eva
Bahn-Vorhersage adds the same core plus, since September 2023, the sequence of DB's own delay forecasts per stop at one-minute resolution (the forecast-evolution series)
2. Live Timetables API (IRIS) — what the archives were built from

Trip label: category (ICE/RE/S), number, operator, flags (long-distance / regional / S-Bahn)
Arrival and departure blocks: planned time, planned platform, planned path (all stops), line; changed time, changed platform, changed path, changed status (cancelled/added), cancellation time, hidden flag, wing-train links
Messages: numeric cause code (e.g., preceding-train delay, construction, signalling failure, staff shortage), message type, validity from/to, priority, category, sometimes free text — your real text annotations
Only the next ~18 hours; history must be archived (piebro's raw parquet keeps the raw XML)
3. Station master data (StaDa) — lookups

Station number, EVA ids, category 1–7, coordinates, state, and facility flags: stepless access (yes/partial/no), mobility service and its hours, toilets, lockers, parking, bicycle parking, taxi rank, WiFi, DB Lounge, travel centre, local staff, 3S emergency centre, plus Ril100 codes and platform lists.

4. Facility status (FaSta) — a live 0/1 series

Facility id, type (elevator/escalator), state (active/inactive/unknown), state explanation, location text ("zu Gleis 4"), station number, coordinates.

5. Coach sequence (Wagenreihung) — lookups

Coach order and type, platform section letters, features: wheelchair space, bike coach, quiet zone, first class, direction of travel.

6. Timetable (GTFS via DELFI/Mobilithek) — structure and accessibility

routes (route_type: rail, bus, tram, subway…), trips (wheelchair_accessible, bikes_allowed), stop_times (planned arrival/departure, stop_sequence, pickup/drop-off rules), stops (wheelchair_boarding, parent_station), transfers (min_transfer_time), calendar and calendar_dates (holidays). GTFS-RT adds per-stop delay updates and service alerts with cause, effect, active period and description text.

How they combine

Group 1 gives series and labels; group 2 gives cause text; groups 3–6 give the static facts on the journey card; group 4 is the one extra series worth adding.

content.text: Three research agents are still running. Meanwhile, four decisions genuinely change the pipeline's shape, and they're independent of what the agents find — let me settle them now.

questions.question: How broad should the agentic discovery layer be? (This is the explicit bonus-point item: "agentic pipelines for automated search, assessment, selection, retrieval, or validation of datasets are a plus".)

options.label: Tiered: generic discovery + DB adapters (Recommended)
options.description: A domain-agnostic agent tier that searches open catalogs (HuggingFace, Zenodo, CKAN/GovData.de, Mobilithek, DB Open-Data) and scores candidates against a machine-readable data spec — plus hand-written retrieval adapters for the DB sources you already know you need. You demo the generic tier rediscovering the DB sources on its own, which is the strongest jury story, and the adapters guarantee you actually have data if discovery underdelivers.

options.label: DB-specific only
options.description: Skip the generic catalog crawler. Hardcode adapters for piebro/HuggingFace, Timetables API, StaDa, FaSta, GTFS. Fastest and lowest-risk in ~21h, but forfeits the headline bonus criterion — the 'agentic' part would only be the annotation step.

options.label: Fully generic, no DB specialization
options.description: Build only the domain-agnostic discovery/assessment/retrieval engine and let it find whatever it finds. Maximum reusability claim, but you risk arriving at training time with a dataset nobody vetted, and the traveller demo gets weaker.

questions.question: What should the model actually predict and explain? This becomes the label + the rationale target.

options.label: Will this connection hold? (Recommended)
options.description: Binary label computed from the data (actual arrival of train A + transfer time ≤ actual departure of train B), with a reasoning trace. Maps exactly onto the deck's flagship output shape — STATE SUMMARY / RECOMMENDED ACTION / EXPECTED OUTCOME — and the accessibility angle (lift status, platform change) makes it a real user problem, not a toy.

options.label: How late will this train be at stop N?
options.description: Bucketed or regression delay forecast at a future stop, with rationale. Simpler labelling and closer to classic forecasting, but the output is a number rather than a decision, so the 'recommend an action' half of the deck's template is harder to demo.

options.label: Is this station/route degrading right now?
options.description: Ops-facing anomaly triage over station-level aggregate series. Good fit for the 'industrial monitoring' framing, but the target user is DB staff rather than a traveller, and you lose the crisp per-connection ground truth.

questions.question: How should the chain-of-thought rationales be generated? This is the expensive step and the main hallucination risk.

options.label: Grounded templates + LLM paraphrase (Recommended)
options.description: Compute the facts deterministically (medians, trend, tail risk, lift state, platform-change rate), fill a reasoning template, then have an LLM rewrite it into natural prose. The LLM never invents a number, so rationales can't contradict the series — and it's cheap enough to annotate the whole training set, not a sample.

options.label: Pure LLM synthesis, as in the OpenTSLM paper
options.description: Feed the series statistics and context to a strong LLM and let it write the full reasoning trace, then filter. Most natural-sounding output and closest to the published recipe, but costs real money at scale and needs a verifier pass to catch rationales whose stated numbers don't match the series.

options.label: Deterministic templates only, no LLM
options.description: Skip generation entirely; emit templated reasoning text. Free, instant, zero hallucination, fully reproducible — but the rationales are visibly formulaic, which the jury may read as not really doing the annotation work.

questions.question: How much data should the pipeline actually process end to end?

options.label: Focused slice, streaming-capable design (Recommended)
options.description: Target one corridor or the top ~20 stations over ~6-12 months. Build the pipeline on DuckDB/Parquet so it streams and would scale, but only materialize the slice. Keeps iteration fast enough to actually finish training and evaluation before the deadline, and gives clean leakage-controlled splits.

options.label: Full available history, all stations
options.description: Ingest everything piebro publishes. Best coverage claim and most training samples, but multi-GB downloads plus a much longer build→train loop, on a deadline where you still need training, evaluation and a demo.

options.label: Tiny fixed sample, hand-picked
options.description: A few hundred connections at one or two stations. Fastest possible path to a working demo, but too small for a credible baseline comparison, which is an explicit submission requirement.

input.description: Design route-plan series schema
input.prompt:
Design task for a 24h hackathon (Temporal AI Challenge, ETH Agentic Systems Lab / Aionic Labs / Nebius). Submission deadline 2026-09-13T10:00Z; it is now ~2026-09-12 evening. Do NOT write files. Return a design, not code. Research is already done — everything you need is below. Do not re-research; spend your effort on design.

## The goal
An **agentic data retrieval pipeline** that produces a TimeNet-conformant dataset for training an OpenTSLM time-series language model on Deutsche Bahn data. The product question the trained model must answer: **"suggest a realistic route plan from A to B, grounded in the historic time series of the varying factors along that route."** Output shape mirrors the organisers' flagship slide: STATE SUMMARY → RECOMMENDED ACTION → EXPECTED OUTCOME, via step-by-step reasoning.

## THE DESIGN FORK I need you to resolve — this is your main job

A teammate already built a pipeline on branch `origin/db-train-idea` that deliberately models **per-station hourly aggregates**, not per-train-run sequences. His stated reason (verbatim from his README): *"A single run visits ten to thirty stops at irregular spacing. A patch encoder has nothing to grip there, and a baseline that lists the numbers as text would match it. A station's hourly curve is dense and strongly seasonal, so the temporal model earns its place. The measured daily cycle runs from about 2 minutes at 06:00 to about 6.5 in the evening, with a second overnight peak."* He explicitly cut "per-train-run sequences across stops" in `not-building.md`.

But a route plan A→B is inherently about legs and transfers, not one station.

Resolve this. My working hypothesis, which you should critique hard and improve or replace: **a route is a sequence of legs; each leg and transfer is grounded in the dense per-station-hourly series (at the transfer stations) plus a per-line-hourly series (for the line operating the leg). So the sample keeps dense, seasonal, patch-friendly series while answering a route-level question.** A candidate itinerary A→B with 1-2 transfers becomes N series (e.g. 3 channels × {origin station, transfer station, destination station} + per-line delay series), all hourly, all 168h context.

Address concretely:
- How many series per training sample, and exactly what each one is. (OpenTSLM constraint: each series strictly 1-D; multivariate = N separate captioned series. Memory scales badly with N×L for the SoftPrompt variant; the Flamingo variant is flat in memory. Sample counts in the paper ranged 1-12 series.)
- What is the label/target? A route plan is generative, not a class. Options to weigh: (a) rank/choose among K candidate itineraries with the label = which one actually performed best historically; (b) scalar prediction of realistic door-to-door arrival time or required buffer minutes; (c) classification of a recommended action (take the direct train / take the earlier connection / allow N min buffer); (d) a composite where a ClassificationTask picks the itinerary and an AnswerTask carries the prose plan. Recommend one primary + note which secondary tasks ride along on the same record.
- How to compute ground truth from historical data without leakage.
- How the fixed context window (168 hourly steps) relates to a specific departure datetime.
- Whether candidate itineraries come from GTFS (gtfs.de static, no credentials, `stop_times`/`transfers.min_transfer_time`) or are derived from observed train runs in the delay data itself. Weigh both.

## Hard constraints from TimeNet (the required output format)
- `BaseConnector` subclass: implement `download(cache_dir) -> list[raw_ref]` (I/O only) and `convert(raw_refs) -> TimeFDataset` (CPU only, no network). Folder `datasets/<org>/<name>/{__init__.py, connector.py, dataset.yaml, requirements.txt, tests/}`, ending `CONNECTOR = MyClass`. Build: `timenet-build --quiet build <id> --out <dir>`. Python 3.11+.
- `dataset.yaml` card is JSON-Schema validated with `additionalProperties: false`. Required: `dataset_id` (`org/name`), `dataset_version` (semver), `name`, `description`, `license` (enum incl. `CC-BY-4.0`). Optional: `domains` (enum incl. `transport`), `tags`, `source_url`, `citation`, `access`.
- Model: Dataset → Record → {TimeSeries, Annotation, Task}. **A record has NO metadata slot** — static facts are `Annotation(key=..., value=...)` with no span. Splits are a static annotation `Annotation(key="split", value="train"|"validation"|"test")`.
- `TimeSeries.from_values(values, spec=TimeSeriesSpec(spec_type=, name=, unit_value=ureg.X), signal=, time_axis=RegularAxis.from_rate_hz(Fraction(1,3600)), time_series_id=)`. Every signal of a modality shares ONE spec; they differ by `signal`.
- Tasks: `ClassificationTask(target=str, target_schema=)`, `AnswerTask(target=str)`, `ScalarPredictionTask(target=float, unit=, target_name=)`. **`rationale: str` is on the Task base class — any task can carry chain-of-thought.** A task answers either inline via `target` or by reference via `target_annotation_ids`, never both.
- `dataset.set_task_stream(...)` exists for datasets with far more tasks than records.
- **TimeNet stores archival raw** — no resampling, no normalization. All preprocessing happens at load time in the adapter.

## Hard constraints from OpenTSLM (the training consumer)
A training sample is exactly 5 keys: `pre_prompt` (str), `time_series_text` (list[str], one caption per series), `time_series` (list of 1-D numeric arrays, positionally aligned with the captions), `post_prompt` (str), `answer` (str). Rules:
- Each series strictly 1-D, non-empty, numeric; **z-scored per series in the dataset class**, and the caption MUST carry the pre-normalization scale: `"<description>, it has mean {mean:.4f} and std {std:.4f}:"` — that caption is the only channel through which absolute scale reaches the model.
- Max 4096 samples per series (1024 patches × patch_size 4); right-zero-padded to a multiple of 4; no padding mask.
- `answer` = the rationale paragraph ending in `Answer: <label>`, plus EOS. Prompts instruct: single natural paragraph, no bullets, don't name the label until the last sentence.
- Integration = subclass `QADataset` implementing `_load_splits`, `_get_answer`, `_get_pre_prompt`, `_get_post_prompt`, `_get_text_time_series_prompt_list`; then register a stage in `curriculum_learning.py`.

## The paper's rationale recipe (arXiv 2510.02410), which we are adapting
GPT-4o (`gpt-4o-2024-08-06`, temp 0.3, seed 42) was shown a **rendered plot** of the unnormalized series plus the correct label, and asked to write the reasoning. Key trick: **answer-set narrowing** — each call is a binary discrimination between the correct label and a deliberately dissimilar distractor from a hand-written dissimilarity map, so rationales stay grounded; at training time the model faces the full label set. Prompts ban referring to the plot, ban stating uncertainty, demand one paragraph, demand the final line be `Answer: [CORRECT]`.
**Our chosen variant** (user decision, already made): grounded templates + LLM paraphrase — compute every number deterministically, fill a reasoning template, have an LLM rewrite into natural prose so it can never invent a number. Design the template slots for the route-plan target.

## What already exists on `origin/db-train-idea` (reuse, do not duplicate)
- `extract.py` — DuckDB `httpfs` reads the HF parquet **in place over HTTPS**, no download: `https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data/resolve/main/monthly_processed_data/data-{YYYY-MM}.parquet`. Aggregates to per-station-hourly `mean_delay`, `cancel_rate`, `trains`. Uses only 5 columns so DuckDB fetches only those byte ranges — a month costs seconds.
- `windows.py` — `CONTEXT_HOURS=168, HORIZON_HOURS=24, STRIDE_HOURS=24, FORECAST_HOURS=6, MAX_IMPUTED_FRACTION=0.10`, channels `(mean_delay, cancel_rate, trains)`; deterministic targets + three template rationale writers.
- `timef.py` — builds the `TimeFDataset`: `RegularAxis.from_rate_hz(Fraction(1,3600))`, specs for delay(minute)/cancellation-rate/throughput, `dataset_id="error404/db-delay-hourly"`, one record per window, three tasks per record.
- `timef_bridge.py` — **the generic TimeF→OpenTSLM adapter** (`rows_from_timef`, `class TimeFQADataset(QADataset)`), z-normalises and emits `"{label}, it has mean {mean:.4f} and std {std:.4f}:"`. Upstream provides no such bridge; this is the reusable-connector bonus item.
- `prepare.py` — 3 months, 40 stations, **2×2 leakage grid**: every 5th station held out × early/late time period, 168h embargo, four eval cells.
- `train_minimal.py` — OpenTSLMSP + LoRA on `google/gemma-3-270m`, scores vs persistence and majority-class baselines.
- `test_db_delay.py` — 7 offline tests on synthetic DuckDB data.

## Available data sources
No credentials, instantly usable: piebro HF parquet (225.8M rows, 67.6GB, CC BY 4.0, columns incl. `station_name`, `eva`, `train_number`, `line_number`, `final_destination_station`, `delay_in_min`, `time`, `arrival_is_canceled`, `departure_is_canceled`, `train_type`, `train_line_ride_id`, `train_line_station_num`, `arrival_planned_time`, `arrival_change_time`, `departure_planned_time`, `departure_change_time`; plus a `raw_data/` partition holding the **raw IRIS XML** from which `ppth` path, platform `pp`/`cp`, and `m@c` cause codes can be recovered); gtfs.de static GTFS (`download.gtfs.de/germany/{fv_free,rv_free}/latest.zip`, daily, next 30 days, CC BY 4.0) with `stop_times`, `transfers.min_transfer_time`, `stops.platform_code`, `trips.wheelchair_accessible`; gtfs.de GTFS-Realtime protobuf (no key).
Needs registration (medium risk in 24h): DB API Marketplace — Timetables/IRIS (~18h horizon, no history), StaDa (station accessibility flags incl. `hasSteplessAccess` yes/no/partial), FaSta (live elevator/escalator state, no history).
Skip: Mobilithek (high registration friction), Wagenreihung/RIS (partner contract).

## Compute
Nebius: platform `gpu-l40s-a` (L40S 48GB) at $1.55/GPU-hour, preset `1gpu-8vcpu-32gb`, image `pytorch/pytorch:2.7.1-cuda12.8-cudnn9-runtime`, $1000 voucher. Code reaches the job as `injectedFiles` (≤64 KiB each) or an S3 bucket mounted as a volume; outputs to a bucket mounted at `/outputs`.

## Deliver
1. Your resolution of the design fork, with reasoning, including the exact list of series per sample and the exact task objects (types, prompts, targets, rationale slots).
2. The agentic pipeline stages: what each agent/stage does, what it emits, and where determinism replaces the LLM. Note explicitly which stages satisfy the organisers' bonus criterion "agentic pipelines for automated search, assessment, selection, retrieval, or validation of datasets", and how a generic (domain-agnostic) discovery tier over open data catalogs plugs in above the DB-specific adapters.
3. The leakage-control design for a route-level target (stations, lines, time — a route shares stations with other routes, so the teammate's per-station holdout may not transfer cleanly; say what breaks and fix it).
4. The riskiest assumptions, and a fallback if the route-plan target proves too ambitious before the deadline.
5. A rough hour-by-hour ordering for what remains, assuming ~19 hours and that the teammate's per-station pipeline already works end to end.

Be concrete and opinionated. Prefer one recommended path over a survey.

questions.question: Your teammate Jonas already pushed a working TimeNet→OpenTSLM pipeline on `origin/db-train-idea` (~950 lines: DuckDB extract, windowing, TimeFDataset builder, the OpenTSLM bridge, leakage grid, LoRA training, 7 tests). How should the agentic retrieval pipeline relate to it?

options.label: Layer on top, reuse his core (Recommended)
options.description: Build the agentic discovery/assessment/validation tier as a new feature that emits the same TimeFDataset shape and feeds his existing bridge and training script. You keep his working end-to-end path as the floor, and the agentic layer is pure upside — which is exactly how the bonus criterion is worded. Needs a decision + owners.md entry, since AGENTS.md §3 says don't edit another person's files.

options.description: Edit extract.py / timef.py / windows.py in place to add the route-level series and tasks. Tighter integration and no duplication, but it collides with his ownership and with his explicit 'not-building' cut of per-run sequences — so it needs him to agree first.

options.description: Build the route-plan pipeline standalone and only converge at the TimeNet dataset boundary. Maximum freedom and no coordination cost now, but you'd rewrite a working DuckDB extractor and OpenTSLM bridge with under a day left.

questions.question: Route planning A→B needs series per leg, but Jonas deliberately modelled per-station hourly aggregates (his reason: per-run sequences are too short and irregular for a patch encoder, so a text baseline would match them). How should a route sample be built?

options.label: Route = legs, each grounded in station+line hourly series (Recommended)
options.description: Keep the dense, seasonal 168h hourly series that make the temporal encoder earn its place, but attach several per sample: the hourly curves at origin, each transfer station, and destination, plus a per-line hourly delay curve for each leg. Answers a route-level question without reintroducing the short irregular sequences he cut.

options.label: Per-run sequences along the route
options.description: Model the actual train run stop-by-stop as the series, which is the most literal reading of 'factors along the route'. But it revives exactly the failure mode he documented — 10-30 irregular stops give a patch encoder little to grip, and a plain text baseline may match it, which would undercut the whole 'the connector earns its place' argument.

options.label: Single fused corridor series
options.description: Aggregate the whole A→B corridor into one set of hourly channels. Fewest series per sample, cheapest memory, simplest to build — but transfers become invisible, and transfer risk is most of what makes a route plan realistic.

input.message:
TWO CORRECTIONS from the user. Adjust your design accordingly — the rest of your brief stands.

**Correction 1 — build standalone, on our own branch.** Do NOT design this as a layer on top of the teammate's `db-train-idea` modules. We converge with his work only at the TimeNet dataset boundary (both emit a valid `TimeFDataset` / built TimeF version directory, both are consumable by the same OpenTSLM `QADataset` bridge pattern). Treat his code as a *reference implementation to learn the API shape from and to benchmark against*, not as a dependency we import. Assume a separate feature directory and a separate git branch, no edits to his files. That means our pipeline needs its own extract path — but note the DuckDB-httpfs-over-HTTPS trick against the HF parquet is a public technique, not his IP, and we should use it too.

**Correction 2 — this is the big one: MULTI-TIMESCALE, chosen empirically.** The user's reasoning, in their words: *"Different lengths of time in the timeline should be chosen because the factors or causes of delays can change according to different times. For example, snow or weather factors, or even construction, which happened in the last month but was not there 3 months ago. I want different types of timelines. For now at least 2 to 3 different types of datasets with different timelines and then whichever performs better on our testing data gets chosen."*

So the deliverable is **not one dataset**. It is a pipeline **parameterized over a "timeline profile"** that emits 2-3 (or more) sibling TimeNet datasets, which are then run through an identical train+eval harness and compared on the same held-out cells. The bake-off result is itself part of the submission story.

Design this explicitly:
- Define the concrete profiles. My starting sketch, which you should critique and refine: **S** = hourly × 168 steps (7 days) — daily + weekly rush-hour cycle, matches the teammate's config so it doubles as the comparison point; **M** = 6-hourly × ~360 steps (90 days) — construction works, timetable changes, multi-week degradation; **L** = daily × 365 steps (1 year) — seasonal and weather regimes. Sanity-check each against the OpenTSLM hard cap of **4096 samples per series** (1024 patches × patch_size 4) — note hourly × 1 year = 8760 is over the cap, so long horizons force coarser resolution, and that tradeoff should be stated in the design.
- Consider adding a **fourth "multi-scale" variant** where S, M and L series are all attached to the *same* record as separate captioned series (OpenTSLM natively takes N series per sample). This is nearly free once the other three exist and may well win. Say whether you'd include it and why.
- How does the resampling/aggregation stage stay one code path across profiles rather than three? What exactly is the profile config object?
- Does the label/target stay identical across profiles (it must, for the comparison to be valid)? If a profile's horizon makes a target ill-defined, say so and say how you'd handle it.
- Coverage constraint: piebro covers the ~100 busiest stations from **2024-07**, all stations only from **2025-11-02**; it is now 2026-09. So the L profile is only viable on the top-100 station set. Factor this in.
- Leakage control must now hold **across profiles as well as within** — the same station/time held out in every profile, or the comparison is meaningless. Say how you guarantee that.
- Extend your hour-by-hour ordering: building 3-4 dataset variants and running 3-4 train/eval runs in ~19h on a single L40S is the schedule risk. Sequence it, and say what gets dropped first if you run late.

The route-plan target and the per-station-vs-per-leg question from my original brief still stand — resolve it as before, but resolve it *once*, so the same record shape is emitted at every timescale.

input.content:
# Agentic data retrieval pipeline → TimeNet → OpenTSLM (Deutsche Bahn route planning)

## Context

The Temporal AI Challenge (ETH Agentic Systems Lab / Aionic Labs / Nebius) asks teams to
source open time-series data, connect it through **TimeNet**, and fine-tune a **TSLM** that
reasons over temporal signals in language. Two of the organisers' criteria are explicitly
about *data*, not modelling:

- Slide 13, step 01: *"Where useful, build an agentic pipeline to search, assess, select,
  retrieve, or validate datasets."*
- Slide 14, bonus: *"Well-chosen datasets and reusable TimeNet connectors that others can
  build on"* and *"Agentic pipelines for automated search, assessment, selection, retrieval,
  or validation of datasets are a plus."*

This plan covers **only that half**: the pipeline that ends with validated TimeNet datasets
plus the documented handoff into training. It does not plan the training run itself beyond
the interface, and it does not plan the demo UI.

The product question the eventual model answers: **"suggest a realistic route plan from A to B,
grounded in the historic behaviour of the factors along that route."** Output mirrors the
organisers' flagship slide — STATE SUMMARY → RECOMMENDED ACTION → EXPECTED OUTCOME, reached
by step-by-step reasoning.

Two user decisions shape the architecture:

1. **Standalone, on its own branch.** A teammate (Jonas) has a working per-station-hourly
   pipeline on `origin/db-train-idea`. We do not import or edit it. We converge only at the
   TimeNet dataset boundary and use his numbers as the comparison point.
2. **Multi-timescale bake-off.** Delay causes live at different timescales — rush hour is
   daily, construction is monthly, weather and timetable changes are seasonal. The pipeline is
   parameterized over a **timeline profile** and emits several sibling datasets; the one that
   wins on held-out data is the one we ship.

Deadline is **2026-09-13T10:00Z**, roughly 19 hours out.

---

## What already exists, and what it means for us

Verified against the repo and upstream sources:

| Thing | State | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `app/agents/` | Empty placeholder. `requires-python = ">=3.10"`, `dependencies = []`, `_hackos_placeholder` comment | We own it. Must delete that comment or `bootstrap.sh` skips installs. Bump to `>=3.11` (TimeNet's floor) |
| `app/backend/.../training-jobs/` | Merged on `main`, working. Nebius submit/wait/logs, `gpu-l40s-a` @ $1.55/GPU-h, injected files ≤64 KiB, S3 volumes, `/outputs` | Training submission is already solved. Do not rebuild it |
| `origin/db-train-idea` | Jonas: DuckDB extract, 168h windows, `TimeFDataset` builder, **TimeF→OpenTSLM bridge**, 2×2 leakage grid, LoRA training, 7 tests | Reference + benchmark. Not a dependency |
| TimeNet | Real, separate from OpenTSLM: `github.com/OpenTSLM/TimeNet`. Python 3.11+ | Our output format. See contract below |
| TimeNet→OpenTSLM bridge | **Does not exist upstream.** TimeNet: *"TimeNet hands you the data and stops there."* OpenTSLM datasets each load their own source | This gap is the reusable-connector bonus. Ours must be domain-agnostic |
| Local toolchain | `uv` 0.11.29, pyenv 3.14.4, brew python3.12, Node 25.9, 285 GiB free. System python3 is 3.9.6 — too old | Pin with `uv python pin 3.12` |

**Sharpest external constraint:** OpenTSLM caps a series at **4096 samples** (1024 patches ×
patch_size 4) and it is a hard `raise`, not a truncation. Hourly × 1 year = 8760 exceeds it.
Long horizons force coarser resolution — this drives the profile table below.

---

## Data sources

**Use (no credentials, works right now):**

- **`piebro/deutsche-bahn-data`** on HuggingFace — 225.8 M rows, 67.6 GB Parquet, CC BY 4.0.
  `monthly_processed_data/data-YYYY-MM.parquet` carries `station_name`, `eva`, `train_number`,
  `line_number`, `delay_in_min`, `time`, `arrival_is_canceled`, `departure_is_canceled`,
  `train_type`, **`train_line_ride_id`**, **`train_line_station_num`**, and the four
  planned/changed arrival/departure timestamps. `raw_data/` keeps the original IRIS XML, from
  which platform `pp`/`cp` and the `m@c` cause codes can be recovered.
  Coverage: ~100 busiest stations from **2024-07**; all stations only from **2025-11-02**.
- **gtfs.de static** — `download.gtfs.de/germany/{fv_free,rv_free}/latest.zip`, CC BY 4.0,
  daily. Gives `transfers.min_transfer_time`, `stops.platform_code`, `wheelchair_boarding`.
  Caveat: covers the **next 30 days only**, so it cannot reconstruct historical itineraries —
  it is enrichment, not ground truth.

**Register in parallel, treat as upside:** DB API Marketplace (Timetables/IRIS for a live demo
layer, StaDa for `hasSteplessAccess`, FaSta for live lift state). Self-service but manual.

**Skip:** Mobilithek (registration friction too high for the window), Wagenreihung/RIS
(partner contract, not self-service).

Because GTFS has no history, **itineraries are reconstructed from the delay data itself**:
`train_line_ride_id` + `train_line_station_num` recover each real run's ordered stop sequence,
and a transfer is feasible when actual arrival + buffer ≤ actual departure. This removes the
GTFS dependency from the critical path entirely.

---

## The pipeline

Ten stages, modelled on how large-scale text pipelines are built (crawl → filter → dedupe →
extract → clean → licence → annotate → curate → validate → document), applied to time series.
**LLM calls appear in exactly three stages (1, 2c, 7); everything else is deterministic** so it
is reproducible and cheap to re-run.

### Stage 0 — SPEC · `spec.py` → `spec.json`
Turn the product question into a machine-readable `DataSpec`: required signals and units,
minimum coverage span, acceptable resolutions, entity keys, licence allowlist, geography,
forecast horizon. Everything downstream scores against this object. Deterministic; the LLM only
drafts it once and a human freezes it.

### Stage 1 — DISCOVER (agentic, generic tier) · `discover/`
Catalog crawlers emitting uniform candidate records
`{source, id, url, title, description, licence, size_bytes, last_modified, format}`:
HuggingFace datasets API, Zenodo API, CKAN endpoints (GovData.de and regional portals),
DB Open-Data portal, GitHub code search. The LLM's only job here is expanding the `DataSpec`
into query terms per catalog; the crawling and pagination are plain HTTP.

This tier is **domain-agnostic** — it takes a `DataSpec` and returns candidates. The DB-specific
adapters in Stage 4 sit *below* it. The demo moment is watching it rediscover
`piebro/deutsche-bahn-data` from the spec alone.

### Stage 2 — ASSESS · `assess/` → `candidates.jsonl`
Three tiers, cheapest first, each culling before the next:

- **2a metadata filter** (free): licence in allowlist, size band, format supported, recency.
- **2b structural probe** (bytes, not files): read a Parquet **footer via HTTP range request**,
  or the first N rows of a CSV. Detect a timestamp column, numeric measures, an entity key.
  Measure sampling regularity, missingness, coverage span, entity cardinality. A candidate that
  has no time column, or spans less than the spec's minimum, dies here without downloading.
- **2c LLM adjudication** (only for ambiguous survivors): does this dataset actually answer the
  spec's question? Returns a rubric score plus a one-line reason.

### Stage 3 — SELECT · `selection.md`
Rank, dedupe near-identical mirrors (a HF mirror of a GitHub release is one dataset), pick.
Write the reasoning for **every** accept *and reject*. The rejection log is the artifact that
proves the pipeline assessed rather than guessed — it is what gets shown to the jury.

### Stage 4 — RETRIEVE · `retrieve/`
One adapter per selected source, with checksums, resume, rate-limit respect, and the licence
file captured alongside the data. The piebro adapter uses **DuckDB `httpfs` to query the
monthly Parquet in place over HTTPS** — column pruning means only the needed byte ranges move,
so a month costs seconds and nothing lands on disk. (Public technique; also what Jonas uses.)

### Stage 5 — ALIGN · `align/` — *profile-parameterized, the one place timescale enters*
The panel → series transform:
1. Reconstruct runs from `train_line_ride_id` + `train_line_station_num`.
2. Enumerate candidate itineraries A→B in a departure window using **planned** times and
   ≤2 transfers, capped at K candidates — this is what a traveller would have seen.
3. Build the aggregate grids per the active **timeline profile**: resample to the profile's
   step, mark a `present` mask, impute (interpolate rate-like channels, zero the count channel),
   and drop any window over the imputed-fraction ceiling.

One code path; the profile is a config object, never a branch.

### Stage 6 — LABEL · `label/`
Replay each candidate with **actual** times: did each transfer hold, what was the real arrival,
which candidate was genuinely best that day. Emit the label plus every number the rationale will
later cite. Purely arithmetic, so the ground truth is objective and needs no hand annotation.

### Stage 7 — NARRATE · `narrate/` — grounded templates + LLM paraphrase
1. Fill a reasoning template from Stage 6's computed facts.
2. An LLM rewrites it into a single natural paragraph, following the paper's prompt discipline:
   no bullets, never mention the answer before the last sentence, never express uncertainty,
   end with `Answer: <label>`.
3. **Verifier** re-extracts every number and claim from the prose and asserts it matches the
   computed facts. Mismatch → retry once, then fall back to the template text.

The LLM never sees a number it is allowed to change, so a rationale cannot contradict its
series. This is a deliberate departure from the paper's GPT-4o-reads-a-plot recipe (which the
authors themselves flag as a limitation: *"we generated CoT datasets using GPT-4o on plots,
which we have shown to perform poorly on these plots alone"*).

### Stage 8 — EMIT · the TimeNet connector
`BaseConnector` subclass producing a `TimeFDataset`. Contract below.

### Stage 9 — VALIDATE · `validate/` → `validation.json`
TimeNet's own card/type/task validation, plus ours: **leakage assertions** (no station, line or
time bucket crosses a split), series finiteness, **length ≤ 4096**, rationale↔target coherence
re-checked post-build, class balance, per-profile coverage report. A failure here fails the
build; this is the "validate datasets" half of the bonus criterion.

### Stage 10 — DOCUMENT · `dataset-card.md`
Generate the datasheet from the manifest + selection log + validation report. **This is a
submission requirement** ("Dataset documentation"), so it is a pipeline output, not an
afterthought.

---

## Timeline profiles — the bake-off

The pipeline emits sibling datasets differing **only** in the profile. Identical target,
identical splits, identical narration templates, so the comparison is valid.

| Profile | Step | Steps | Span | Captures | Station set |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **S** | 1 h | 168 | 7 days | Daily + weekly rush-hour cycle | all |
| **M** | 6 h | 360 | 90 days | Construction, timetable changes, multi-week degradation | all |
| **L** | 1 day | 365 | 1 year | Seasonal and weather regimes | **top-100 only** |
| **MS** | mixed | S+M+L attached to one record as separate captioned series | multi-scale | — | top-100 only |

Notes that drive the table:
- Every row is under the 4096 cap. Hourly × 1 year (8760) is not, which is *why* L is daily.
- **L and MS are limited to the top-100 station set** — piebro only covers all stations from
  2025-11-02, and a 1-year window needs history back to 2025-09.
- **MS is nearly free** once S/M/L exist (OpenTSLM takes N series per sample natively) and is a
  plausible winner, since it is the only variant that can see a monthly regime shift *and* the
  daily cycle. Include it if the schedule holds; it is the first thing to cut if not.
- Profiles share one `TimelineProfile` config object: `{step, n_steps, channels,
  max_imputed_fraction, station_set}`. Stage 5 reads it; no other stage knows about timescale.

**Leakage must hold across profiles, not just within.** The holdout station set and the
train/test time boundary are computed **once**, from the profile-independent station and date
universe, and passed into every build. If each profile picked its own split, a station held out
in S but trained on in M would make the bake-off meaningless. The embargo between train and test
is sized to the **longest** profile's context (365 days for L), applied to all, so no profile
gets a shorter effective gap than another.

---

## The TimeNet contract (what Stage 8 must produce)

Verified against the TimeNet source, not the docs — `docs/connectors.md` describes a flat-file
layout that the code does not use.

**Folder** — `datasets/<org>/<name>/` with `__init__.py` (re-exports `CONNECTOR`),
`connector.py` (ends `CONNECTOR = OurClass`), `dataset.yaml`, `requirements.txt`, `tests/`.
Discovery is lazy by dataset id, org lowercased and leaf hyphens → underscores. There is no
central registry to edit.

**`dataset.yaml`** is JSON-Schema validated with **`additionalProperties: false`** — any extra
key is a hard failure. Required: `dataset_id` (`org/name`), `dataset_version` (semver), `name`,
`description`, `license` (enum; `CC-BY-4.0` is valid). Optional: `domains` (enum includes
`transport`), `tags`, `source_url`, `citation`, `access`.

**Two methods:** `download(cache_dir) -> list[raw_ref]` (I/O only, idempotent, no parsing) and
`convert(raw_refs) -> TimeFDataset` (CPU only, no network). Connectors take **no constructor
arguments** — configuration comes from environment variables. Since our profile must reach the
connector, the profile id is an env var read in `__init__`, and each profile is its own
`dataset_id` (`error404/db-route-s`, `-m`, `-l`, `-ms`).

**Object model** — Dataset → Record → {TimeSeries, Annotation, Task}:
- `TimeSeries.from_values(values, spec=..., signal=..., time_axis=..., time_series_id=...)`.
  All signals of a modality **share one `TimeSeriesSpec`** and differ by `signal`.
  Axis: `RegularAxis.from_rate_hz(Fraction(1, 3600))` for hourly — it takes a `Fraction`, not a
  float, deliberately.
- **A record has no metadata slot.** Static facts (station, line, itinerary description,
  and the **split**) are `Annotation(key=..., value=...)` with no span. `split` as an annotation
  is the documented convention and our leakage-control mechanism.
- Tasks: `ClassificationTask(target=str, target_schema=...)`, `ScalarPredictionTask(target=float,
  unit=..., target_name=...)`, `AnswerTask(target=str)`. **`rationale: str` is on the Task base
  class**, so any task carries chain-of-thought — no special CoT type. A task answers either
  inline via `target` or by reference via `target_annotation_ids`, never both.
- **TimeNet stores archival raw** — no resampling, no normalization, native units. All
  z-scoring and padding happens later, in the load-time adapter.

**Build:** `timenet-build --quiet build <id> --out <dir>` (the `--quiet` belongs to the tool,
not the subcommand). Then `TimeNet(<dir>).load(<id>).describe()` to confirm.

---

## Handoff into training (how TimeNet feeds OpenTSLM)

There is no upstream bridge. Ours is a `QADataset` subclass whose `_load_splits()` calls
`TimeNet().load(dataset_id)` and partitions records by the `split` annotation. It is
**domain-agnostic by construction** — it reads records, series and tasks, so any TimeF dataset
can train an OpenTSLM model. That reusability is the bonus-point claim.

An OpenTSLM sample is exactly five keys, and the conversion is:

| OpenTSLM key | Built from |
| --- | --- |
| `pre_prompt` | `task.prompt` + resolved `input_annotation_ids` (origin/destination/departure context) + instruction block |
| `time_series_text[i]` | `spec.name` / `signal` / unit **+ the pre-normalization mean and std** |
| `time_series[i]` | `series.to_numpy()` → z-score per series → `list[float]`, one per series |
| `post_prompt` | the candidate-itinerary option list + `You MUST end your response with "Answer: "` |
| `answer` | `task.rationale` + `Answer: {task.target}` + EOS |

Non-negotiable details, each verified in the OpenTSLM source:
- Every series **strictly 1-D**. Multivariate = N separate captioned series, never a 2-D array.
- Series are z-scored **in the dataset class**, and the caption carries mean/std in the format
  `"<description>, it has mean {mean:.4f} and std {std:.4f}:"`. That caption is the **only**
  channel through which absolute scale reaches the model — get it wrong and the model cannot
  tell 2 minutes late from 20.
- `time_series_text[i]` and `time_series[i]` are **positionally aligned**.
- Right-zero-padded to a multiple of 4, no padding mask (tolerable only because post-z-score
  zero is the series mean).
- `QADataset` **caches all three splits on the class at first instantiation** — the first
  `EOS_TOKEN` wins for every split. Instantiate deliberately.

**Model choice:** OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt memory grows with series count × length (87 GB peak on
12-lead ECG); **Flamingo is flat** (~20 GB for Llama-1B across the whole sweep). With 7+ series
per sample the MS profile is a SoftPrompt OOM risk on a 48 GB L40S. Start SP on profile S,
switch to Flamingo if MS OOMs.

**Nebius:** the pipeline runs locally and uploads the built TimeF directory to an Object Storage
bucket; the training job mounts it (`--volume bucket:/data --output bucket`). Code reaches the
job as injected files (≤64 KiB each) or from the same bucket. Do **not** try to stream the HF
parquet from inside the job — keep extraction local and reproducible.

---

## Files

New feature, own branch, no edits to Jonas's tree:

```
app/agents/src/features/db_route/
  spec.py            DataSpec + the frozen spec.json
  profiles.py        TimelineProfile config objects (S, M, L, MS)
  discover/          catalog crawlers (HF, Zenodo, CKAN, GitHub) — generic tier
  assess/            2a metadata filter · 2b parquet-footer probe · 2c LLM adjudication
  select.py          ranking, mirror dedupe, selection.md writer
  retrieve/          piebro (DuckDB httpfs) · gtfs (zip) · cache + checksums
  align/             run reconstruction · itinerary enumeration · profile-driven gridding
  label.py           actual-time replay, ground truth, rationale facts
  narrate/           templates · LLM paraphrase · numeric verifier
  timenet/           <org>/<name>/{__init__,connector,dataset.yaml,requirements.txt,tests}
  bridge.py          TimeF → OpenTSLM QADataset (domain-agnostic)
  validate.py        leakage + shape + coherence assertions
  bakeoff.py         run all profiles through one train/eval harness, emit the comparison
  tests/             offline, synthetic, no network
```

Also: delete the `_hackos_placeholder` comment in `app/agents/pyproject.toml`, declare deps
(`duckdb`, `numpy`, `pyarrow`, `timenet[build]`, `timenet-connectors`, `opentslm`, `torch`),
bump `requires-python` to `>=3.11`, and wire the pipeline's smoke command into
`team-setup/scripts/smoke.sh` (its EDIT-ME block currently runs the backend tests only, and
AGENTS.md §9 says "unconfigured is not a pass").

**Coordination, before writing code** — AGENTS.md §3 forbids editing another person's files and
`owners.md` is currently blank: record a decision in `decisions.md`
(`- [d-<uuid>] [T+HH:MM] … — promotes [i-e77e2fbe…]`, the existing "agentic pipeline" idea line)
and claim `app/agents/src/features/db_route/` in `owners.md`. Jonas already logged the agentic
pipeline as a raised idea, so this is adoption, not a land grab.

---

## Verification

Offline first — every test runs on synthetic data with no network:

1. `python -m pytest app/agents/src/features/db_route/tests` — gridding is correct at each
   profile step; itinerary enumeration finds known chains in a fixture; label replay matches
   hand-computed ground truth; the narration verifier **rejects** a rationale with a tampered
   number; no station, line or time bucket crosses a split, **in every profile**; every series
   is finite and ≤ 4096 samples.
2. `uv run timenet-build --quiet build error404/db-route-s --out /tmp/reg` then
   `python -c "from timenet.client import TimeNet; TimeNet('/tmp/reg').load('error404/db-route-s').describe()"`
   — proves the card validates and the manifest round-trips.
3. `python -m db_route.bridge --smoke` — print one assembled OpenTSLM sample and assert the five
   keys, 1-D series, aligned captions carrying mean/std, and an `answer` ending
   `Answer: <label><eos>`.
4. Discovery dry-run: `python -m db_route.discover --spec spec.json --dry-run` returns
   `piebro/deutsche-bahn-data` in the top results, and `selection.md` explains the rejects.
5. End-to-end on one month, one profile, small station set — build → validate → 20 training
   steps on CPU — before spending any Nebius time.
6. Then the real run: `npm --prefix app/backend run train submit …` per profile, and
   `bakeoff.py` emits the comparison table against the persistence and majority-class baselines.

---

## Sequencing (~19 h) and the cut list

| Hours | Work |
| --- | --- |
| 0–1 | Branch, ownership decision, deps declared, `uv python pin 3.12`, TimeNet + OpenTSLM installed and importable. Start the DB Marketplace registration now so it ripens in the background |
| 1–4 | Stages 4–6: retrieve → align → label for **profile S**. Offline tests alongside |
| 4–6 | Stage 7 narration + verifier; Stage 8 connector; first `timenet-build` green |
| 6–8 | `bridge.py` + Stage 9 validation. **Checkpoint: one profile trains end to end on CPU** |
| 8–10 | Profiles M and L — config only if Stage 5 was written properly |
| 10–13 | Nebius runs per profile; `bakeoff.py` comparison |
| 13–15 | Stages 1–3 (discovery/assess/select) — the bonus tier, built last because it is upside, not critical path |
| 15–17 | MS profile if the schedule held; Stage 10 dataset card |
| 17–19 | Buffer, demo, evidence and limitations write-up |

**Cut in this order if late:** MS profile → L profile → the LLM adjudication tier in 2c (keep the
deterministic 2a/2b probe, which is most of the value) → GTFS enrichment. **Never cut:** the
narration verifier, the leakage assertions, or the dataset card — those are correctness and
submission requirements, not features.

**Riskiest assumptions**, flagged rather than hidden:
- That itinerary reconstruction from `train_line_ride_id` yields enough clean A→B chains at the
  chosen stations. Probe this in hour 1 with a single SQL query before building on it — if it is
  thin, fall back to a fixed set of busy corridors.
- That the route-level target does not dilute the series signal enough to let a text baseline
  match it (Jonas's documented concern about per-run sequences, which is why we keep dense
  aggregate series rather than stop-by-stop ones). The bake-off measures this directly; if the
  no-connector baseline matches us on every profile, that is a finding to report honestly, and
  the per-station target remains as the fallback.
- That one L40S fits four train/eval runs in the window. It probably does not at full size —
  hence the cut order above.

ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)"
cd "$ROOT" || exit 1

STATE_DIR="team-setup/state"
SMOKE_HEAD="$(git rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null || true)"
SMOKE_DIRTY="$(git status --porcelain -- app 2>/dev/null || true)"
export SMOKE_HEAD SMOKE_DIRTY
OK=1
DETAIL=""

if [ -n "$SMOKE_HEALTH_URL" ]; then
  if command -v curl >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    RESPONSE="$(curl --max-time 20 -sf "$SMOKE_HEALTH_URL" 2>&1)"

    fi
  else
    OK=0
    DETAIL="curl not found, cannot check SMOKE_HEALTH_URL"

if [ -n "$SMOKE_COMMAND" ]; then

fi

# Agentic data retrieval pipeline → TimeNet → OpenTSLM (Deutsche Bahn route planning)

## Context

The Temporal AI Challenge (ETH Agentic Systems Lab / Aionic Labs / Nebius) asks teams to
source open time-series data, connect it through **TimeNet**, and fine-tune a **TSLM** that
reasons over temporal signals in language. Two of the organisers' criteria are explicitly
about *data*, not modelling:

- Slide 13, step 01: *"Where useful, build an agentic pipeline to search, assess, select,
  retrieve, or validate datasets."*
- Slide 14, bonus: *"Well-chosen datasets and reusable TimeNet connectors that others can
  build on"* and *"Agentic pipelines for automated search, assessment, selection, retrieval,
  or validation of datasets are a plus."*

This plan covers **only that half**: the pipeline that ends with validated TimeNet datasets
plus the documented handoff into training. It does not plan the training run itself beyond
the interface, and it does not plan the demo UI.

The product question the eventual model answers: **"suggest a realistic route plan from A to B,
grounded in the historic behaviour of the factors along that route."** Output mirrors the
organisers' flagship slide — STATE SUMMARY → RECOMMENDED ACTION → EXPECTED OUTCOME, reached
by step-by-step reasoning.

Two user decisions shape the architecture:

1. **Standalone, on its own branch.** A teammate (Jonas) has a working per-station-hourly
   pipeline on `origin/db-train-idea`. We do not import or edit it. We converge only at the
   TimeNet dataset boundary and use his numbers as the comparison point.
2. **Multi-timescale bake-off.** Delay causes live at different timescales — rush hour is
   daily, construction is monthly, weather and timetable changes are seasonal. The pipeline is
   parameterized over a **timeline profile** and emits several sibling datasets; the one that
   wins on held-out data is the one we ship.

Deadline is **2026-09-13T10:00Z**, roughly 19 hours out.

---

## What already exists, and what it means for us

Verified against the repo and upstream sources:

| Thing | State | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `app/agents/` | Empty placeholder. `requires-python = ">=3.10"`, `dependencies = []`, `_hackos_placeholder` comment | We own it. Must delete that comment or `bootstrap.sh` skips installs. Bump to `>=3.11` (TimeNet's floor) |
| `app/backend/.../training-jobs/` | Merged on `main`, working. Nebius submit/wait/logs, `gpu-l40s-a` @ $1.55/GPU-h, injected files ≤64 KiB, S3 volumes, `/outputs` | Training submission is already solved. Do not rebuild it |
| `origin/db-train-idea` | Jonas: DuckDB extract, 168h windows, `TimeFDataset` builder, **TimeF→OpenTSLM bridge**, 2×2 leakage grid, LoRA training, 7 tests | Reference + benchmark. Not a dependency |
| TimeNet | Real, separate from OpenTSLM: `github.com/OpenTSLM/TimeNet`. Python 3.11+ | Our output format. See contract below |
| TimeNet→OpenTSLM bridge | **Does not exist upstream.** TimeNet: *"TimeNet hands you the data and stops there."* OpenTSLM datasets each load their own source | This gap is the reusable-connector bonus. Ours must be domain-agnostic |
| Local toolchain | `uv` 0.11.29, pyenv 3.14.4, brew python3.12, Node 25.9, 285 GiB free. System python3 is 3.9.6 — too old | Pin with `uv python pin 3.12` |

**Sharpest external constraint:** OpenTSLM caps a series at **4096 samples** (1024 patches ×
patch_size 4) and it is a hard `raise`, not a truncation. Hourly × 1 year = 8760 exceeds it.
Long horizons force coarser resolution — this drives the profile table below.

---

## Data sources

**Use (no credentials, works right now):**

- **`piebro/deutsche-bahn-data`** on HuggingFace — 225.8 M rows, 67.6 GB Parquet, CC BY 4.0.
  `monthly_processed_data/data-YYYY-MM.parquet` carries `station_name`, `eva`, `train_number`,
  `line_number`, `delay_in_min`, `time`, `arrival_is_canceled`, `departure_is_canceled`,
  `train_type`, **`train_line_ride_id`**, **`train_line_station_num`**, and the four
  planned/changed arrival/departure timestamps. `raw_data/` keeps the original IRIS XML, from
  which platform `pp`/`cp` and the `m@c` cause codes can be recovered.
  Coverage: ~100 busiest stations from **2024-07**; all stations only from **2025-11-02**.
  *Verified live during planning:* public, ungated, last modified 2026-09-12, and the resolve
  URL returns `accept-ranges: bytes` — so the footer-probe and DuckDB range-read techniques both
  work. `data-2026-08.parquet` is 595 MB, which is why column pruning is not optional.
- **gtfs.de static** — `download.gtfs.de/germany/{fv_free,rv_free}/latest.zip`, CC BY 4.0,
  daily. Gives `transfers.min_transfer_time`, `stops.platform_code`, `wheelchair_boarding`.
  Caveat: covers the **next 30 days only**, so it cannot reconstruct historical itineraries —
  it is enrichment, not ground truth.

**Register in parallel, treat as upside:** DB API Marketplace (Timetables/IRIS for a live demo
layer, StaDa for `hasSteplessAccess`, FaSta for live lift state). Self-service but manual.

**Skip:** Mobilithek (registration friction too high for the window), Wagenreihung/RIS
(partner contract, not self-service).

Because GTFS has no history, **itineraries are reconstructed from the delay data itself**:
`train_line_ride_id` + `train_line_station_num` recover each real run's ordered stop sequence,
and a transfer is feasible when actual arrival + buffer ≤ actual departure. This removes the
GTFS dependency from the critical path entirely.

---

## The pipeline

Ten stages, modelled on how large-scale text pipelines are built (crawl → filter → dedupe →
extract → clean → licence → annotate → curate → validate → document), applied to time series.
**LLM calls appear in exactly three stages (1, 2c, 7); everything else is deterministic** so it
is reproducible and cheap to re-run.

### Stage 0 — SPEC · `spec.py` → `spec.json`
Turn the product question into a machine-readable `DataSpec`: required signals and units,
minimum coverage span, acceptable resolutions, entity keys, licence allowlist, geography,
forecast horizon. Everything downstream scores against this object. Deterministic; the LLM only
drafts it once and a human freezes it.

### Stage 1 — DISCOVER (agentic, generic tier) · `discover/`
Catalog crawlers emitting uniform candidate records
`{source, id, url, title, description, licence, size_bytes, last_modified, format}`:
HuggingFace datasets API, Zenodo API, CKAN endpoints (GovData.de and regional portals),
DB Open-Data portal, GitHub code search. The LLM's only job here is expanding the `DataSpec`
into query terms per catalog; the crawling and pagination are plain HTTP.

This tier is **domain-agnostic** — it takes a `DataSpec` and returns candidates. The DB-specific
adapters in Stage 4 sit *below* it. The demo moment is watching it rediscover
`piebro/deutsche-bahn-data` from the spec alone.

### Stage 2 — ASSESS · `assess/` → `candidates.jsonl`
Three tiers, cheapest first, each culling before the next:

- **2a metadata filter** (free): licence in allowlist, size band, format supported, recency.
- **2b structural probe** (bytes, not files): read a Parquet **footer via HTTP range request**,
  or the first N rows of a CSV. Detect a timestamp column, numeric measures, an entity key.
  Measure sampling regularity, missingness, coverage span, entity cardinality. A candidate that
  has no time column, or spans less than the spec's minimum, dies here without downloading.
- **2c LLM adjudication** (only for ambiguous survivors): does this dataset actually answer the
  spec's question? Returns a rubric score plus a one-line reason.

### Stage 3 — SELECT · `selection.md`
Rank, dedupe near-identical mirrors (a HF mirror of a GitHub release is one dataset), pick.
Write the reasoning for **every** accept *and reject*. The rejection log is the artifact that
proves the pipeline assessed rather than guessed — it is what gets shown to the jury.

### Stage 4 — RETRIEVE · `retrieve/`
One adapter per selected source, with checksums, resume, rate-limit respect, and the licence
file captured alongside the data. The piebro adapter uses **DuckDB `httpfs` to query the
monthly Parquet in place over HTTPS** — column pruning means only the needed byte ranges move,
so a month costs seconds and nothing lands on disk. (Public technique; also what Jonas uses.)

### Stage 5 — ALIGN · `align/` — *profile-parameterized, the one place timescale enters*
The panel → series transform:
1. Reconstruct runs from `train_line_ride_id` + `train_line_station_num`.
2. Enumerate candidate itineraries A→B in a departure window using **planned** times and
   ≤2 transfers, capped at K candidates — this is what a traveller would have seen.
3. Build the aggregate grids per the active **timeline profile**: resample to the profile's
   step, mark a `present` mask, impute (interpolate rate-like channels, zero the count channel),
   and drop any window over the imputed-fraction ceiling.

One code path; the profile is a config object, never a branch.

### Stage 6 — LABEL · `label/`
Replay each candidate with **actual** times: did each transfer hold, what was the real arrival,
which candidate was genuinely best that day. Emit the label plus every number the rationale will
later cite. Purely arithmetic, so the ground truth is objective and needs no hand annotation.

### Stage 7 — NARRATE · `narrate/` — grounded templates + LLM paraphrase
1. Fill a reasoning template from Stage 6's computed facts.
2. An LLM rewrites it into a single natural paragraph, following the paper's prompt discipline:
   no bullets, never mention the answer before the last sentence, never express uncertainty,
   end with `Answer: <label>`.
3. **Verifier** re-extracts every number and claim from the prose and asserts it matches the
   computed facts. Mismatch → retry once, then fall back to the template text.

The LLM never sees a number it is allowed to change, so a rationale cannot contradict its
series. This is a deliberate departure from the paper's GPT-4o-reads-a-plot recipe (which the
authors themselves flag as a limitation: *"we generated CoT datasets using GPT-4o on plots,
which we have shown to perform poorly on these plots alone"*).

### Stage 8 — EMIT · the TimeNet connector
`BaseConnector` subclass producing a `TimeFDataset`. Contract below.

### Stage 9 — VALIDATE · `validate/` → `validation.json`
TimeNet's own card/type/task validation, plus ours: **leakage assertions** (no station, line or
time bucket crosses a split), series finiteness, **length ≤ 4096**, rationale↔target coherence
re-checked post-build, class balance, per-profile coverage report. A failure here fails the
build; this is the "validate datasets" half of the bonus criterion.

### Stage 10 — DOCUMENT · `dataset-card.md`
Generate the datasheet from the manifest + selection log + validation report. **This is a
submission requirement** ("Dataset documentation"), so it is a pipeline output, not an
afterthought.

---

## Timeline profiles — the bake-off

The pipeline emits sibling datasets differing **only** in the profile. Identical target,
identical splits, identical narration templates, so the comparison is valid.

| Profile | Step | Steps | Span | Captures | Station set |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **S** | 1 h | 168 | 7 days | Daily + weekly rush-hour cycle | all |
| **M** | 6 h | 360 | 90 days | Construction, timetable changes, multi-week degradation | all |
| **L** | 1 day | 365 | 1 year | Seasonal and weather regimes | **top-100 only** |
| **MS** | mixed | S+M+L attached to one record as separate captioned series | multi-scale | — | top-100 only |

Notes that drive the table:
- Every row is under the 4096 cap. Hourly × 1 year (8760) is not, which is *why* L is daily.
- **L and MS are limited to the top-100 station set** — piebro only covers all stations from
  2025-11-02, and a 1-year window needs history back to 2025-09.
- **MS is nearly free** once S/M/L exist (OpenTSLM takes N series per sample natively) and is a
  plausible winner, since it is the only variant that can see a monthly regime shift *and* the
  daily cycle. Include it if the schedule holds; it is the first thing to cut if not.
- Profiles share one `TimelineProfile` config object: `{step, n_steps, channels,
  max_imputed_fraction, station_set}`. Stage 5 reads it; no other stage knows about timescale.

**Leakage must hold across profiles, not just within.** The holdout station set and the
train/test time boundary are computed **once**, from the profile-independent station and date
universe, and passed into every build. If each profile picked its own split, a station held out
in S but trained on in M would make the bake-off meaningless. The embargo between train and test
is sized to the **longest** profile's context (365 days for L), applied to all, so no profile
gets a shorter effective gap than another.

---

## The TimeNet contract (what Stage 8 must produce)

Verified against the TimeNet source, not the docs — `docs/connectors.md` describes a flat-file
layout that the code does not use.

**Folder** — `datasets/<org>/<name>/` with `__init__.py` (re-exports `CONNECTOR`),
`connector.py` (ends `CONNECTOR = OurClass`), `dataset.yaml`, `requirements.txt`, `tests/`.
Discovery is lazy by dataset id, org lowercased and leaf hyphens → underscores. There is no
central registry to edit.

**`dataset.yaml`** is JSON-Schema validated with **`additionalProperties: false`** — any extra
key is a hard failure. Required: `dataset_id` (`org/name`), `dataset_version` (semver), `name`,
`description`, `license` (enum; `CC-BY-4.0` is valid). Optional: `domains` (enum includes
`transport`), `tags`, `source_url`, `citation`, `access`.

**Two methods:** `download(cache_dir) -> list[raw_ref]` (I/O only, idempotent, no parsing) and
`convert(raw_refs) -> TimeFDataset` (CPU only, no network). Connectors take **no constructor
arguments** — configuration comes from environment variables. Since our profile must reach the
connector, the profile id is an env var read in `__init__`, and each profile is its own
`dataset_id` (`error404/db-route-s`, `-m`, `-l`, `-ms`).

**Object model** — Dataset → Record → {TimeSeries, Annotation, Task}:
- `TimeSeries.from_values(values, spec=..., signal=..., time_axis=..., time_series_id=...)`.
  All signals of a modality **share one `TimeSeriesSpec`** and differ by `signal`.
  Axis: `RegularAxis.from_rate_hz(Fraction(1, 3600))` for hourly — it takes a `Fraction`, not a
  float, deliberately.
- **A record has no metadata slot.** Static facts (station, line, itinerary description,
  and the **split**) are `Annotation(key=..., value=...)` with no span. `split` as an annotation
  is the documented convention and our leakage-control mechanism.
- Tasks: `ClassificationTask(target=str, target_schema=...)`, `ScalarPredictionTask(target=float,
  unit=..., target_name=...)`, `AnswerTask(target=str)`. **`rationale: str` is on the Task base
  class**, so any task carries chain-of-thought — no special CoT type. A task answers either
  inline via `target` or by reference via `target_annotation_ids`, never both.
- **TimeNet stores archival raw** — no resampling, no normalization, native units. All
  z-scoring and padding happens later, in the load-time adapter.

**Build:** `timenet-build --quiet build <id> --out <dir>` (the `--quiet` belongs to the tool,
not the subcommand). Then `TimeNet(<dir>).load(<id>).describe()` to confirm.

---

## Handoff into training (how TimeNet feeds OpenTSLM)

There is no upstream bridge. Ours is a `QADataset` subclass whose `_load_splits()` calls
`TimeNet().load(dataset_id)` and partitions records by the `split` annotation. It is
**domain-agnostic by construction** — it reads records, series and tasks, so any TimeF dataset
can train an OpenTSLM model. That reusability is the bonus-point claim.

An OpenTSLM sample is exactly five keys, and the conversion is:

| OpenTSLM key | Built from |
| --- | --- |
| `pre_prompt` | `task.prompt` + resolved `input_annotation_ids` (origin/destination/departure context) + instruction block |
| `time_series_text[i]` | `spec.name` / `signal` / unit **+ the pre-normalization mean and std** |
| `time_series[i]` | `series.to_numpy()` → z-score per series → `list[float]`, one per series |
| `post_prompt` | the candidate-itinerary option list + `You MUST end your response with "Answer: "` |
| `answer` | `task.rationale` + `Answer: {task.target}` + EOS |

Non-negotiable details, each verified in the OpenTSLM source:
- Every series **strictly 1-D**. Multivariate = N separate captioned series, never a 2-D array.
- Series are z-scored **in the dataset class**, and the caption carries mean/std in the format
  `"<description>, it has mean {mean:.4f} and std {std:.4f}:"`. That caption is the **only**
  channel through which absolute scale reaches the model — get it wrong and the model cannot
  tell 2 minutes late from 20.
- `time_series_text[i]` and `time_series[i]` are **positionally aligned**.
- Right-zero-padded to a multiple of 4, no padding mask (tolerable only because post-z-score
  zero is the series mean).
- `QADataset` **caches all three splits on the class at first instantiation** — the first
  `EOS_TOKEN` wins for every split. Instantiate deliberately.

**Model choice:** OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt memory grows with series count × length (87 GB peak on
12-lead ECG); **Flamingo is flat** (~20 GB for Llama-1B across the whole sweep). With 7+ series
per sample the MS profile is a SoftPrompt OOM risk on a 48 GB L40S. Start SP on profile S,
switch to Flamingo if MS OOMs.

**Nebius:** the pipeline runs locally and uploads the built TimeF directory to an Object Storage
bucket; the training job mounts it (`--volume bucket:/data --output bucket`). Code reaches the
job as injected files (≤64 KiB each) or from the same bucket. Do **not** try to stream the HF
parquet from inside the job — keep extraction local and reproducible.

---

## Files

New feature, own branch, no edits to Jonas's tree:

```
app/agents/src/features/db_route/
  spec.py            DataSpec + the frozen spec.json
  profiles.py        TimelineProfile config objects (S, M, L, MS)
  discover/          catalog crawlers (HF, Zenodo, CKAN, GitHub) — generic tier
  assess/            2a metadata filter · 2b parquet-footer probe · 2c LLM adjudication
  select.py          ranking, mirror dedupe, selection.md writer
  retrieve/          piebro (DuckDB httpfs) · gtfs (zip) · cache + checksums
  align/             run reconstruction · itinerary enumeration · profile-driven gridding
  label.py           actual-time replay, ground truth, rationale facts
  narrate/           templates · LLM paraphrase · numeric verifier
  timenet/           <org>/<name>/{__init__,connector,dataset.yaml,requirements.txt,tests}
  bridge.py          TimeF → OpenTSLM QADataset (domain-agnostic)
  validate.py        leakage + shape + coherence assertions
  bakeoff.py         run all profiles through one train/eval harness, emit the comparison
  tests/             offline, synthetic, no network
```

Also: delete the `_hackos_placeholder` comment in `app/agents/pyproject.toml`, declare deps
(`duckdb`, `numpy`, `pyarrow`, `timenet[build]`, `timenet-connectors`, `opentslm`, `torch`),
bump `requires-python` to `>=3.11`, and wire the pipeline's smoke command into
`team-setup/scripts/smoke.sh` (its EDIT-ME block currently runs the backend tests only, and
AGENTS.md §9 says "unconfigured is not a pass").

**Coordination, before writing code** — AGENTS.md §3 forbids editing another person's files and
`owners.md` is currently blank: record a decision in `decisions.md`
(`- [d-<uuid>] [T+HH:MM] … — promotes [i-e77e2fbe…]`, the existing "agentic pipeline" idea line)
and claim `app/agents/src/features/db_route/` in `owners.md`. Jonas already logged the agentic
pipeline as a raised idea, so this is adoption, not a land grab.

---

## Verification

Offline first — every test runs on synthetic data with no network:

1. `python -m pytest app/agents/src/features/db_route/tests` — gridding is correct at each
   profile step; itinerary enumeration finds known chains in a fixture; label replay matches
   hand-computed ground truth; the narration verifier **rejects** a rationale with a tampered
   number; no station, line or time bucket crosses a split, **in every profile**; every series
   is finite and ≤ 4096 samples.
2. `uv run timenet-build --quiet build error404/db-route-s --out /tmp/reg` then
   `python -c "from timenet.client import TimeNet; TimeNet('/tmp/reg').load('error404/db-route-s').describe()"`
   — proves the card validates and the manifest round-trips.
3. `python -m db_route.bridge --smoke` — print one assembled OpenTSLM sample and assert the five
   keys, 1-D series, aligned captions carrying mean/std, and an `answer` ending
   `Answer: <label><eos>`.
4. Discovery dry-run: `python -m db_route.discover --spec spec.json --dry-run` returns
   `piebro/deutsche-bahn-data` in the top results, and `selection.md` explains the rejects.
5. End-to-end on one month, one profile, small station set — build → validate → 20 training
   steps on CPU — before spending any Nebius time.
6. Then the real run: `npm --prefix app/backend run train submit …` per profile, and
   `bakeoff.py` emits the comparison table against the persistence and majority-class baselines.

---

## Sequencing (~19 h) and the cut list

| Hours | Work |
| --- | --- |
| 0–1 | Branch, ownership decision, deps declared, `uv python pin 3.12`, TimeNet + OpenTSLM installed and importable. Start the DB Marketplace registration now so it ripens in the background |
| 1–4 | Stages 4–6: retrieve → align → label for **profile S**. Offline tests alongside |
| 4–6 | Stage 7 narration + verifier; Stage 8 connector; first `timenet-build` green |
| 6–8 | `bridge.py` + Stage 9 validation. **Checkpoint: one profile trains end to end on CPU** |
| 8–10 | Profiles M and L — config only if Stage 5 was written properly |
| 10–13 | Nebius runs per profile; `bakeoff.py` comparison |
| 13–15 | Stages 1–3 (discovery/assess/select) — the bonus tier, built last because it is upside, not critical path |
| 15–17 | MS profile if the schedule held; Stage 10 dataset card |
| 17–19 | Buffer, demo, evidence and limitations write-up |

**Cut in this order if late:** MS profile → L profile → the LLM adjudication tier in 2c (keep the
deterministic 2a/2b probe, which is most of the value) → GTFS enrichment. **Never cut:** the
narration verifier, the leakage assertions, or the dataset card — those are correctness and
submission requirements, not features.

**Riskiest assumptions**, flagged rather than hidden:
- That itinerary reconstruction from `train_line_ride_id` yields enough clean A→B chains at the
  chosen stations. Probe this in hour 1 with a single SQL query before building on it — if it is
  thin, fall back to a fixed set of busy corridors.
- That the route-level target does not dilute the series signal enough to let a text baseline
  match it (Jonas's documented concern about per-run sequences, which is why we keep dense
  aggregate series rather than stop-by-stop ones). The bake-off measures this directly; if the
  no-connector baseline matches us on every profile, that is a finding to report honestly, and
  the per-station target remains as the fallback.
- That one L40S fits four train/eval runs in the window. It probably does not at full size —
  hence the cut order above.
